opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, deep learning research has always been bottlenecked less by ideas and more by execution. Most researchers have far more hypotheses than they can ever test. You think of ten things worth trying, and in practice you get to maybe two of them, because each one means writing code, debugging infrastructure, babysitting runs, reading through logs, and figuring out whether a result is real or just a bug. A huge fraction of a researcher's week goes to that kind of work.

What's changed over the last couple of years is that coding models have gotten genuinely good. They're no longer just autocomplete. They can take a fairly underspecified task, go off, write a substantial amount of code, run it, notice it's broken, fix it, and come back with something that works. Once you have that, the obvious question is: what happens if you point that capability at the research process itself?

So I see two reasons it's promising. The first is leverage. If a single researcher can direct many agents running experiments in parallel, the number of ideas you can actually test goes up by an order of magnitude, maybe more. Research is a search process, and search gets much better when each step is cheaper.

The second reason is more fundamental. There's a feedback loop here. Better models make better coding agents, better coding agents make research faster, and faster research makes better models. I think we're at the point where that loop is starting to close in a real way, not just in theory. If you believe that, then the most important thing you can do is build an organization where that loop is the central design principle rather than an afterthought.

That's hard to do inside an existing lab. Big labs have established workflows, codebases, and team structures built around humans doing the work, and retrofitting automation onto that is slow. Starting fresh lets you ask from day one: if agents are doing a large share of the engineering, what should the infrastructure look like, what should a researcher's job be, and how do you measure progress? Those questions are easier to answer from a blank slate.

I don't want to overstate it. The agents still make mistakes, they can be confidently wrong, and research taste, knowing which questions matter, is still very much a human skill. But I think the ceiling on how much automation can accelerate research is much higher than most people assume, and finding out how high it goes seemed like the most exciting thing I could work on.

r001.rationale: The response says a fresh lab can design its workflows and infrastructure around agents from day one, while retrofitting automation into established labs is slow.

r002.rationale: It argues that making experiments cheaper and running many in parallel lets researchers test far more ideas, improving research as a search process.

r003.rationale: It describes a single researcher directing many agents to test far more ideas and presents discovering automation’s potential ceiling as the exciting research challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that deep learning research, the way it's actually practiced day to day, is mostly not the romantic version where you have a brilliant idea and then the idea is the hard part. The hard part is everything around the idea. You have a hypothesis, you need to write the training code, set up the data pipeline, launch the job, wait, discover the job crashed at 3am because of some shape mismatch or a bad checkpoint load, fix it, relaunch, wait again, build the eval harness, realize the eval is measuring the wrong thing, and so on. If you look at how a strong researcher spends their week, maybe ten percent of it is the thinking that only they could do, and ninety percent is this loop of implementation, debugging and plumbing.

And that loop is exactly what coding agents have gotten good at. When I was working on reasoning models and on code, the thing that surprised me was not that models could write a function. It was that they could sit inside a long, messy loop, run things, read the error, try again, and keep going for hours without getting frustrated or bored. That's precisely the shape of experimental work in ML.

So the bet is roughly this. If you can compress that ninety percent, you change the economics of research. A researcher who can run twenty variations of an experiment overnight instead of two learns much faster. Ideas that were never worth trying because the engineering cost was too high suddenly become cheap. You stop pruning your search tree based on how annoying something is to implement and start pruning based on whether it's actually a good idea. I think a lot of research progress is bottlenecked on exactly that, on the number of experiments a small group can realistically run and interpret.

The reason to build a new lab around this rather than just adopting the tools inside an existing one is that it's hard to retrofit. Large labs have workflows, infrastructure and incentives that were all designed around humans doing the loop. If you start fresh, you can design the whole organization assuming the loop is automated from day one. The infrastructure is built for agents to use, not humans. Experiments are logged in a way that a model can read. The research process itself becomes something you can study and improve, which is kind of the point. We want to find out what it looks like when the research pipeline is the thing you're optimizing, not just the model at the end of it.

There's also a more speculative version of the argument that I find motivating. Deep learning has gotten better mostly by scaling things that were already working. There haven't been that many genuinely new ideas relative to the amount of compute poured in. Part of why is that exploring new ideas is expensive and risky for a human career. An agent doesn't care about that. It will happily spend a week on a direction that has a two percent chance of working if you ask it to. If you can make exploration cheap and run a lot of it in parallel, I think you find things that the field has been collectively walking past because nobody could justify the time.

I don't want to oversell it. The agents today still need a lot of hand holding, they make confident mistakes, and the judgment about which experiment matters is still very much a human thing. But the trajectory is clear, and I'd rather be the group that figures out how to work this way early and makes all the mistakes now, than wait until it's obvious and everyone is doing it.

r001.rationale: The response says existing labs are hard to retrofit and describes a new lab designed from day one around automated workflows and infrastructure for agents.

r002.rationale: It argues that running many more experiments faster helps researchers learn faster and explore ideas that were previously too costly to try.

r003.rationale: The response mentions a small group running more experiments and says the research pipeline itself should be studied, but it does not clearly frame the new lab as an experiment in how much a small team can accomplish through agents and automation.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is a particularly good place to start because you have a feedback loop. You can ask a model to write a program, run it, and see whether it works. That doesn’t tell you everything about the quality of the solution, but it gives you a way to learn from outcomes rather than just imitate what people have written.

And coding is also a big part of doing deep learning research. You implement an idea, debug it, run an experiment, look at the results, and decide what to try next. If agents can take on more of that work, you can shorten the time between having a hypothesis and finding out whether it’s useful.

The interesting part is going beyond making individual researchers faster. Can a model carry an experiment through, recognize that the result contradicts its assumptions, and change direction? That requires reasoning over longer periods and learning from failures. So building those agents is itself a research problem, while also giving you tools that could help you make progress on the next research problem. That’s what makes it a promising foundation for a lab.

r001.rationale: The response supports using agents to carry out research work, but does not say workflows should be built natively around them instead of retrofitting existing workflows.

r002.rationale: It says agents could shorten the cycle from a hypothesis to learning whether it is useful, helping researchers decide what to try next.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe the lab as testing what a small team can accomplish with extensive agent use and automation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is a particularly powerful place to start because it gives you a tight feedback loop. A model can write something, run it, see what failed, and try again. That creates an opportunity to learn through interaction, especially as tasks become longer and require more planning.

And coding is also a big part of doing deep learning research. You implement ideas, build experiments, debug infrastructure, and analyze results. If we can make agents useful across that loop, we can help researchers test more ideas and spend more time on the questions that matter.

The exciting part is that those two directions reinforce each other. Building better agents can accelerate research, and that research can help us build better agents. A new lab gives you the opportunity to organize around that feedback loop from the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response says the new lab can organize around the agent feedback loop “from the beginning” and make agents useful across research workflows, conveying a workflow designed around agents at the outset.

r002.rationale: It describes a tight loop of running code, seeing failures, and trying again, then says agents could help researchers test more ideas in deep learning research.

r003.rationale: The response does not frame the lab as an experiment in what a small team can accomplish, or describe extensive use of agents and automation in those terms.
